title: Production Debugging & Observability
summary: You can't attach a debugger to a service handling real traffic. Learn the workflow that replaces stepping through code: logs, metrics, and traces read together, and the discipline of investigating without making things worse.

slides.markdown:
[debugging-tools-techniques](debugging-tools-techniques) assumed you could attach a debugger and step through code. In production, you almost never can — the process is serving real users, pausing it stalls every request it's holding, and there usually isn't a debugger port open on a prod host anyway.

What replaces stepping through code is reading **logs, metrics, and traces together** — the observability data you instrumented in advance, because there's no instrumenting after the fact once the incident is already happening. Production debugging is also higher stakes: every action you take is on a live system with real cost, so "try something and see" carries real blast radius.

This topic covers the workflow this constraint forces: what to look at first, how to reason about a distributed system's complexity, and the discipline of investigating without making the outage worse.

Three constraints that don't exist in dev, all at once:

- **No debugger.** You typically can't attach a debugger to a production process — no port for it, and even where technically possible, pausing a live process to inspect it means every request it's holding stalls, and clients start retrying, doubling load.
- **Real traffic, not a repro.** You can't necessarily reproduce the exact input that triggered the failure; it may depend on a specific customer's data, a specific concurrent timing, or scale you can't recreate locally.
- **Real cost of downtime.** Every minute of investigation is a minute of degraded service for real users, which changes the calculus: mitigating the symptom fast can matter more than understanding the cause immediately.

The skill this demands is different from local debugging: reasoning from indirect evidence (logs and metrics) rather than direct inspection, and being deliberate about actions because you can't easily undo them.

slides.subTitle: Logs, metrics, traces — and what each answers
slides.markdown:
Production observability rests on three complementary data types, each answering a question the others can't:

- **Logs** answer *"what exactly happened, in detail, for this one event or request?"* — rich, high-cardinality, but expensive to query broadly.
- **Metrics** answer *"how is the system behaving in aggregate, and is it getting worse?"* — cheap to store and graph over long time ranges, but they show *that* error rate spiked, not *why*.
- **Traces** answer *"where, across services, did this specific request spend its time or fail?"* — a distributed request's path stitched together (built on the correlation IDs from [reading-stack-traces-and-logs](reading-stack-traces-and-logs)).

A real investigation moves between all three: a metric's dashboard shows *something* is wrong and roughly when; a trace shows *where* in the request path it's concentrated; a log for one specific slow or failing trace shows *exactly what* happened. Any one pillar alone tends to leave a gap the others fill.

Seeing where latency or errors concentrate across a multi-service request makes the value of tracing concrete. A single trace breaks the request into **spans** — one per service or operation — each with its own start time and duration, nested to show which calls happened inside which.

When one span is disproportionately wide compared to its siblings, that's where the time went; when a span's status is an error while its parent succeeded (or vice versa via a fallback), that's where the failure originated. This is exactly the information a stack trace can't give you, because a stack trace only ever covers one process — a trace covers the whole request's journey.

slides.sectionTitle: Dashboards and alerting as the first signal
slides.markdown:
In production, you almost never start an investigation by reading code — you start from a **dashboard or an alert** telling you something is wrong: error rate above threshold, latency p99 climbing, a queue depth growing unbounded.

A good dashboard is built around a small number of high-signal indicators (often the **SLIs** a team already tracks: latency, error rate, saturation) rather than every metric available, so the first glance tells you *whether* something's wrong without hunting through noise. Alerting exists to make that first signal proactive rather than something you discover from a user complaint — the gap between "the metric crossed the threshold" and "a human is looking at it" is often the largest chunk of an incident's total duration.

The dashboard doesn't tell you the cause — it tells you *where to start looking* and *how bad it is*, which is the first two things you need before touching a trace or a log.

slides.sectionTitle: Correlating a spike with a change
slides.markdown:
The single highest-value question when a metric spikes: **what changed right before it?** Most production incidents are triggered by a change, not a spontaneous failure of previously-stable code, because code that's been running unchanged for weeks doesn't usually pick a random Tuesday to break.

The candidates to check, roughly in order of frequency:

- **A deploy** — did this service or one it depends on ship a release in the window before the spike started?
- **A config or feature-flag change** — these bypass code review's usual scrutiny and are a disproportionately common cause.
- **A traffic shift** — a marketing push, a client retry storm, a batch job starting, or a dependency's outage rerouting load onto you.

Overlaying a deploy-marker annotation on the same graph as the error-rate spike is often the fastest single diagnostic step in an incident — if the two lines up, you have a strong hypothesis before reading a single log line.

slides.subTitle: Before touching any state
slides.markdown:
The default posture during investigation is **read-only**: query logs, view metrics, inspect traces, maybe run a read-only database query to check current state — none of which can make the incident worse.

Even "harmless-looking" investigation actions carry risk in production: running an expensive ad-hoc query against the primary database can add load that tips an already-struggling system over; restarting a process "just to see the fresh logs" destroys in-memory state and evidence, and may cause a thundering herd of reconnecting clients; attaching a profiler or debugger to a live process pauses it, stalling every in-flight request.

The practical rule: prefer replicas over primaries for investigative queries, prefer existing dashboards/logs over new instrumentation added live, and if you must run something with any side effect, say out loud (or in the incident channel) what you're about to do and why before doing it — so someone can stop you if it's riskier than you think.

slides.subTitle: Where complexity moves
slides.markdown:
| | Monolith | Distributed system |
|---|---|---|
| Call visibility | One process, one stack trace covers everything | Request spans many processes; no single stack trace shows the whole path |
| Failure mode | Usually fails together, in one place | Partial failures — one dependency down while the rest works, producing confusing mixed symptoms |
| Root cause locality | Often local to the function that threw | May be a dependency two hops away, a network partition, or a shared resource under contention |
| Tooling | Debugger, single-process profiler often suffice | Requires distributed tracing and correlation IDs; a single-process debugger sees only its slice |

The complexity doesn't disappear in a distributed system — it moves from "understanding one big codebase" to "understanding how many small pieces interact under partial failure." A trace that threads a correlation ID across every hop is the distributed-system equivalent of a monolith's single stack trace, which is why it's the first tool reached for once a problem is confirmed to span services.

slides.sectionTitle: Testing a theory live, without a rollback plan
slides.markdown:
Mid-incident, it's tempting to make a live change to confirm a hypothesis — flip a feature flag, bump a timeout, restart a suspect service — and see if the symptom improves. Done without a rollback plan, this routinely turns one incident into two.

What goes wrong in practice: the change has a side effect nobody anticipated (bumping a timeout upstream causes a downstream service to be overwhelmed by requests that previously would have failed fast); the change is applied and nobody records exactly what was changed, so if it needs reverting under pressure ten minutes later, that itself becomes a scramble; or the "test" partially works, muddying the signal so nobody can tell if the original problem or the new change is now the cause of the symptoms being observed.

The fix: before any live change, know exactly how to revert it, say what you're doing and why in the incident channel first, and change one thing at a time so the result is attributable — the same one-variable discipline from [systematic-debugging-method](systematic-debugging-method), just with higher stakes.

slides.sectionTitle: A production investigation, start to finish
slides.markdown:
Putting the pillars together as a workflow: an alert fires on error-rate; the dashboard shows it started 8 minutes ago and is concentrated on one endpoint; you overlay the deploy markers and see a release shipped 10 minutes ago touching that endpoint's service; you pull a trace for a failing request and see the time and the error both concentrated in one downstream span; you pull the logs for that specific span, filtered by the trace's correlation ID, and read the actual exception and its chained cause.

At that point you likely have enough to decide: roll back the deploy (mitigate first, root-cause later — the subject of the next topic) rather than debug forward under pressure. The pillars got you from "something's wrong" to "here's the specific cause" in minutes, entirely through read-only investigation, without ever attaching a debugger to anything.

This topic is the debugging workflow that *consumes* an observability stack; the tooling itself — logging pipelines, metrics/time-series systems, distributed tracing infrastructure, dashboard design, and alerting — is covered in full by System Design's `observability` group and Cloud/DevOps's `observability-ops` group. Read those for how the pillars are built; this topic is how to use them under pressure.

The next topic, [concurrency-bugs-and-heisenbugs](concurrency-bugs-and-heisenbugs), covers a class of bug that makes production debugging even harder: one where the act of observing — adding a log, attaching a profiler — can change or hide the very behavior you're trying to catch. And [on-call-and-incident-response](on-call-and-incident-response) covers the team process this investigation happens inside of: roles, severity, and communication during the incident this workflow is part of.
